Project management assistance based on artificial intelligence and machine learningTechnical Field

The present application relates to project management assistance, and more particularly to project management assistance based on artificial intelligence and machine learning.

Background

Various techniques may be used for project management. Generally with respect to project management, a team may conduct a brainstorming to generate a project plan, identify personnel and equipment required to implement the project plan, set a project schedule, and conduct a continuous meeting to determine the implementation of the project plan. Ongoing conferences may result in modifications to project plans and/or modifications to personnel, equipment, schedules, etc. related to the project plans.

Disclosure of Invention

Embodiments of the present disclosure relate to project management assistance based on artificial intelligence and machine learning. In some examples, the artificial intelligence and machine learning based project management assistance may include ascertaining queries by a user. The query may relate to the item. Attributes associated with the user and attributes associated with the item may be ascertained. Queries can be analyzed based on ascertained attributes associated with users and items. The predictor category may be identified based on the analyzed query from a plurality of predictor categories, wherein the plurality of predictor categories includes a performance predictor category, a quality predictor category, a review predictor category, and a plan predictor category. Predictors from the plurality of predictors can be identified based on the identified predictor category. A response to the query may be generated based on execution of the identified predictor. Further, a display responsive to the query may be generated based on the generated response.

Detailed Description

For purposes of simplicity and illustration, the invention is described primarily by reference to examples. In the following description, numerous specific details are set forth in order to provide a thorough understanding of the present disclosure. It may be evident, however, that the disclosure may be practiced without limitation to these specific details. In other instances, some methods and structures have not been described in detail so as not to unnecessarily obscure the present disclosure.

Throughout this disclosure, the terms "a" and "an" are intended to mean at least one of the specified elements. As used herein, the term "comprising" means including but not limited to, the term "including" means including but not limited to. The term "based on" means based at least in part on.

Disclosed herein are artificial intelligence and machine learning based project management assistance apparatuses, methods for artificial intelligence and machine learning based project management assistance, and non-transitory computer readable media having machine readable instructions stored thereon to provide artificial intelligence and machine learning based project management assistance. The apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer-readable media disclosed herein provide artificial intelligence and machine learning based project management assistance by identifying a predictor category from a plurality of predictor categories for a project, wherein the plurality of predictor categories includes a performance predictor category, a quality predictor category, a review predictor category, and a plan predictor category. Further, predictors from the plurality of predictors can be identified based on the identified predictor categories to respond to user queries to facilitate project management with respect to the project. Item management may be automatically controlled based on execution of the identified predictors to meet the item criteria specified in the query. For example, as disclosed herein, item targets may include specified speeds, throughput, etc. associated with the item. For example, as disclosed herein, project management may be automatically controlled by analyzing aspects such as first-time correct story predictions, story quality predictions, promise accuracy predictions, defect injection predictions, and/or task predictions to modify resources (e.g., equipment, personnel, etc.) assigned to a project and/or schedules associated with the project to meet project criteria specified in a query.

With respect to project management, in the field of software development, one technique includes agile project management. Regarding agile items, various factors may affect agile item management. Examples of factors include: the team's ability to fulfill all commitments, the accuracy of the estimates, the actual extent of the current publication plan, whether the existing process will solve the problem as expected, whether the team speed, the expected growth in speed, whether the upcoming publication will inject defects that may affect product quality, whether the test scenario is valid, whether the requirements are properly sized, whether the problem is properly prioritized, etc.

Regarding the factors described above in connection with agile project management, burn-up (burn down) charts and burn-up (burn up) charts may provide an indication of whether a project goal is ahead of or behind schedule, as well as current and/or desired burn-up rates and burn-up rates. The burnout chart may provide an indication of the amount of work remaining in the project, while the burnout chart may provide an indication of the amount of work completed and the total amount of work. Based on the use of such burnout and burnup charts, as well as other available techniques, it is technically challenging to process the above-described factors associated with agile project management and predict whether the goal is reached.

To address at least the technical challenges described above, the apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer readable media disclosed herein may implement predictive analysis of demand listings and delivery plans to form more accurate estimates. The product demand list may be described as a prioritized list of features, including a brief description of all functions specified for the product. The apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer-readable media disclosed herein may also address technical challenges associated with the engagement of disparate project management systems as compared to known project management techniques. In this regard, the various components of the apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer-readable media disclosed herein may provide a high level of integration that results in increased reliability of the various components by reducing errors, mismatches, and use of memory, storage, and computing resources. Accordingly, the various components of the apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer-readable media disclosed herein may provide reliable project management to meet the project criteria specified in the query as disclosed herein. The various components of the apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer-readable media disclosed herein may also provide reliable synchronization of project standards, project attributes, and project management, thereby preventing mismatches, and thereby effectively and reliably generating responses to queries.

According to an example, the apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer-readable media disclosed herein may implement predictive analysis to combine data for multiple teams to establish accurate delivery plans and more realistic delivery goals.

According to an example, the apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer-readable media disclosed herein may implement predictive analysis to analyze historical data of defects to improve quality of results.

According to another aspect, agility may require timely delivery to gain a competitive advantage in the marketplace. However, it is unknown whether a deliverable product can be delivered before a specified date. In this regard, the apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer readable media disclosed herein may implement predictive analysis by analyzing historical data, capabilities, and throughput to predict the feasibility of immediate delivery.

According to another aspect, agile users may encounter a number of problems to be resolved. However, the agile user may not know which problem may have the greatest impact and should be handled first. In this regard, the apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer readable media disclosed herein may implement predictive analysis to determine which problem will have the greatest impact and should be treated first.

According to an example, the apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer-readable media disclosed herein may implement predictive analysis to analyze historical data to predict a likelihood of future results.

According to an example, the apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer-readable media disclosed herein may implement optimization and simulation techniques to suggest a suggestion for answering "what we should do? "possible consequences of the problem, and performing an analysis of" hypothesis occurrence … … ".

According to an example, the apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer-readable media disclosed herein may provide an opportunity to take precautionary measures to adjust future results according to goals.

According to an example, the apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer-readable media disclosed herein may enable a user (e.g., a product owner) to compare possible future results with a planned product development blueprint and provide an opportunity for realignment.

According to an example, the apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer-readable media disclosed herein may be used whenever a user needs to know about future things, or supplement unavailable information.

According to an example, the apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer-readable media disclosed herein may enable a user (such as a project team leader) to anticipate future results of a agile development team to facilitate continued improvement.

According to an example, the apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer-readable media disclosed herein may enable a user (such as a agile coach) assistance team to first identify and address the most influential problem.

According to an example, the apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer-readable media disclosed herein may implement predictors that may be categorized with respect to performance, quality, review, and planning. In this regard, as disclosed herein, the performance class predictor may include a speed predictor and a throughput predictor. The quality class predictors may include a first correct story predictor, a story quality predictor, and a defect injection predictor. Review category predictors may include a commitment accuracy predictor and a workload distribution predictor. The plan category predictors may include a task predictor and a publication plan feasibility predictor.

The speed predictor may predict speed for all teams or for a particular team, at the project level, for future durations (e.g., weeks). The speed predictor may facilitate (e.g., by the product owner) comparing future speeds to the product development blueprint. The speed predictor may facilitate analysis of future speeds (e.g., by a agile development team) and operate on the analyzed future speeds. Logic associated with the speed predictor may include determining an accumulated speed and a requested speed. The rate of accumulation may be determined based on the total number of story points completed up to the specified date. The required speed may be determined as: the sum of the story points for the complete product demand list is divided by the number of weeks between the first posting start date and the user-provided demand list target date. If a particular team (e.g., the selected team) is selected, the required speed may be determined as: the sum of the story points for the complete product demand list for the selected team divided by the number of weeks between the first publication (for the selected team) start date and the user-provided demand list target date.

The first correct story predictor may predict a first correct story percentage for future releases and sprints. The first correct story predictor may enable continued improvement to improve delivery quality, minimize the number of defects, and reduce the effort to repair and test defects. The first correct story predictor may facilitate improvements in the publishing and sprinting process. Logic associated with the first correct story predictor may include: the first correct story percentage is determined based on the total number of user stories performed without the defect associated therewith divided by the total number of user stories performed.

For the first correct story predictor, a mapping of defects to stories may be performed. In this regard, upon selection (e.g., actuation) of a particular plot point, an option to calibrate and analyze the data may be presented. Upon selection of the calibration option, a circle graph may be displayed to show the percentage distribution of the story point aspects of the particular story. Upon selection of the analyze data option, story data having features such as filtering, sorting, searching, etc. may be displayed.

The story quality predictor may predict the number of defects per story for future releases and spurs. The story quality predictor may facilitate the production of a promulgated product at the end of each sprint and release. The story quality predictor may provide an improvement in story quality. Logic associated with the story quality predictor may include: the flaw of each story is determined from the total number of flaws associated with the story performed for the particular sprint and/or posting divided by the total number of user stories performed for the particular sprint and/or posting.

For a story quality predictor, upon selection (e.g., actuation) of a particular plot point, an option to calibrate and analyze the data may be presented. After selecting the calibration option, a circle graph may be displayed to show a percentage distribution in terms of severity of the particular defect. Upon selection of the analyze data option, defect data having characteristics such as filtering, sorting, searching, etc. may be displayed.

The commitment accuracy predictor may predict a commitment accuracy percentage (e.g., commitment speed versus actual speed) for future releases and sprints. The promise accuracy predictor may provide a comparison of accuracy of estimates using workload (e.g., planned workload versus actual workload) to analyze "what should we do? The "promise accuracy predictor may provide assistance to users (e.g., agile development team) to anticipate future results to prioritize work accordingly. Logic associated with the commitment accuracy predictor may include: the speed estimate accuracy percentage is determined from the total story point completed divided by the total story point promised. Further, the workload estimation accuracy percentage may be determined from the planned total workload divided by the actual total workload. For the promise accuracy predictor, a story-to-task mapping may be performed to determine the planned and actual workload for the story.

The throughput predictor may predict the number of work items for a future week. Throughput predictors can promote consistent and sustainable pace at the product and team level. Logic associated with the throughput predictor may include: the closed work items are determined based on the total number of work items (e.g., stories and defects) closed within the particular week.

The defect injection predictor may predict the number of defects for future sprints and publications. If the predictions exceed allowable limits, the defect injection predictor may assist the team in taking preventive action. The defect injection predictor may facilitate a quick failure concept to shorten the feedback loop. Logic associated with the defect injection predictor may include: the defects of each sprint and/or post are determined based on the total number of defects posed for the story that was made as part of the particular sprint and post.

For the defect injection predictor, a mapping of defects to stories may be performed. For the defect injection predictor, an option to calibrate and analyze the data may be presented when a particular plot point is selected (e.g., actuated). Upon selection of the calibration option, a stacked bar graph may be displayed to illustrate the prioritized closed and open defects. Upon selection of the analyze data option, defect data having characteristics such as filtering, sorting, searching, etc. may be displayed.

The task predictor may predict task types for stories divided in sprints. The task predictor may predict the amount of work required to complete a task (e.g., for a task). The task predictor may facilitate improvement of accuracy of workload estimation by users (e.g., agile development teams).

Task predictors can predict standard tasks or task types based on story types and historical data (such as task titles) by implementing machine learning techniques.

The task predictor may predict the workload (e.g., in hours) for a predicted standard task or task type based on: story type, task type, story points assigned to the respective stories, and actual workload taken for similar tasks. In this regard, similar tasks may include tasks having the same story type, task type, and story point.

With respect to a task type predictor of the task predictor, the task type predictor may utilize input from sprint planning and factors such as user story type. Different usage story types of the story may be added to the selected sprint requirements list. For a task type predictor, historical task titles under similar type stories may be obtained from an associated database. The output of the task type predictor may include a task type.

With respect to the workload predictor of the task predictor, the workload predictor may utilize input from the sprint scheme and factors such as the user story type. Different usage story types of the story may be added to the selected sprint requirements list. The task type may be obtained from a task type predictor and/or sprint plan. The story point may be obtained from a sprint program. In this regard, different and unique story points may be assigned to stories added to the selected sprint range. Further, historical actual workload for similar types of tasks may be obtained from the associated databases. The output of the workload predictor may include the workload (e.g., in hours).

The publication plan feasibility predictor may consider scope, quality, workload, and time to predict the feasibility of a publication plan. The distribution plan feasibility predictor may predict the date when the full scope will be delivered. The distribution plan feasibility predictor may predict the range that may be delivered before a certain date. The publication plan feasibility predictor may predict the quality of future publications. In addition, the publication plan feasibility predictor may facilitate advanced analysis of publication feasibility to take corrective action.

The workload distribution predictor may predict a workload distribution between stories and defects for future releases and/or sprints. The workload distribution predictor may analyze whether a user (e.g., team) will spend more workload on defects rather than stories in upcoming sprites and/or publications.

The apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer readable media disclosed herein may implement adaptive planning on predictive planning.

The apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer-readable media disclosed herein may implement adaptive solutions to support uniqueness of different users (e.g., agile development teams) and products.

The apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer-readable media disclosed herein may predict in advance what will happen for an upcoming (e.g., weeks or months) release of a product, thereby enabling a user (e.g., product owner) to act proactively to provide a competitive advantage.

The apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer-readable media disclosed herein may provide insight that may act to solve a problem before the problem occurs.

The apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer-readable media disclosed herein may provide answers to questions such as "what speed will be", "whether quality will be standard" by reducing interference and uncertainty.

The apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer readable media disclosed herein may predict defects before they occur to thereby eliminate the cost of repairing the defects and increase the value of the product.

The apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer readable media disclosed herein may implement adaptive planning on predictive planning by giving limited priority to adaptive planning based on identifying the actual status and handling the highest level of uncertainty.

For the apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer-readable media disclosed herein, the elements of the apparatus, methods, and non-transitory computer-readable media disclosed herein may be any combination of hardware and programming to implement the functions of the respective elements. In some examples described herein, a combination of hardware and programming may be implemented in a number of different ways. For example, the program for an element may be processor-executable instructions stored on a non-transitory, machine-readable storage medium, and the hardware for the element may include processing resources to execute those instructions. In these examples, a computing device implementing these elements may include a machine-readable storage medium storing instructions and a processing resource executing the instructions, or the machine-readable storage medium may be stored separately and accessed by the computing device and the processing resource. In some examples, some elements may be implemented in circuitry.

FIG. 1 illustrates a layout of an example apparatus (also referred to hereinafter as "apparatus 100") for project management assistance based on artificial intelligence and machine learning.

Referring to fig. 1, apparatus 100 may include a user query analyzer 102 that is executed by at least one hardware processor (e.g., hardware processor 2102 of fig. 21, or hardware processor 2304 of fig. 23) to determine a query 104 by a user 106. The query 104 may be related to the item 108. The user query analyzer 102 may be executed on a first server (not shown) that includes at least one hardware processor and memory (e.g., memory similar to memory 2104 of fig. 21 and/or memory of non-transitory computer-readable medium 2302 of fig. 23).

A user attribute analyzer 110, executed by at least one hardware processor, may ascertain attributes 112 associated with a user 106. For example, the attributes 112 may include the user's position (e.g., a project team leader for the agile project, an agile coach, manager, etc. for the agile project), or the type of user, such as an agile development team for the agile project, a product owner of a product associated with the project 108, etc. The user attribute analyzer 110 may be executed on a first server comprising at least one hardware processor and memory (e.g., memory similar to memory 2104 of fig. 21 and/or memory of non-transitory computer-readable medium 2302 of fig. 23).

Item attribute analyzer 114, executed by at least one hardware processor, can ascertain attributes 116 associated with item 108. For example, the attributes 116 may include the type of item (e.g., agile-based item), details related to the item (e.g., start date, end date, person involved, location, priority associated with the task, task status, task Identification (ID), story ID, sprint ID, etc.), and generally, information related to any item related to the analysis disclosed herein. The item property analyzer 114 may be executed on a first server that includes at least one hardware processor and memory (e.g., memory similar to memory 2104 of fig. 21 and/or memory of non-transitory computer-readable medium 2302 of fig. 23).

A query response generator 118 executed by the at least one hardware processor may analyze the query 104 by the user 106 based on the ascertained attributes 112 associated with the user 106 and the ascertained attributes 116 associated with the item 108. Although the query response generator 118 is shown in fig. 1 as a component of the apparatus 100, alternatively the query response generator 118 may be executed on a second server (not shown) comprising at least one hardware processor and memory (e.g., similar to memory 2104 of fig. 21 and/or memory of non-transitory computer-readable medium 2302 of fig. 23). The second server may be located at a remote site as compared to the first server, and various types of information associated with the components of apparatus 100 may be exchanged between the first server and the second server, for example, over a network or otherwise.

The query response generator 118 may identify a predictor category 120 from a plurality of predictor categories including a performance predictor category 122, a quality predictor category 124, a review predictor category 126, and a plan predictor category 128 based on the analyzed query 104.

The query response generator 118 may identify a predictor 130 from a plurality of predictors based on the identified predictor category 120, the plurality of predictors including: a speed predictor 132 and a throughput predictor 134 of the performance predictor category 122; a first correct story predictor 136, a story quality predictor 138, and a defect injection predictor 140 for quality predictor category 124; a promise accuracy predictor 142 that reviews the predictor category 126; and a task predictor 144 that plans the predictor category 128.

The query response generator 118 may generate a response 146 to the query 104 by the user 106 based on the execution of the identified predictors 130.

A response display generator 148, executed by the at least one hardware processor, may generate a display 150 responsive to the query 104 by the user 106 based on the generated response 146. The response display generator 148 may be executed on a first server including at least one hardware processor and memory (e.g., memory similar to memory 2104 of fig. 21 and/or memory of non-transitory computer-readable medium 2302 of fig. 23).

According to an example, the speed predictor 132 may be executed by at least one hardware processor to determine a speed associated with the item 108 for a future duration based on the accumulated speed and the requested speed. The speed can be described as: such as a measure of how much work a team can do in one iteration. The speed may be measured in stories or story points. The accumulation rate can be described as: such as the sum of the speeds at which a team completes over multiple iterations within a given publication. The required speed can be described as: the team completes at least the average speed required for the remaining "requisite" category user stories in the remaining iterations of a given release so that the smallest marketable product can be deployed into production. In this example, the speed predictor 132 may be executed by at least one hardware processor to determine an accumulated speed from a total number of completed story points up to a specified date, and determine the required speed as the sum of story points for the complete product demand list divided by the duration between the first posting start date and the demand list target date. The story point may represent a unitless measure of relative size assigned to a requirement for a function. The story point may allow a team to focus on delivering the size and complexity of a particular function, rather than trying to perfectly estimate the duration required for its completion. The product demand list may be described as a priority list of functional and non-functional requirements that when implemented will deliver the requirements of the project. The list of product requirements may be divided into the release of suggestions. The release start date may represent the date that the team began processing the submitted/planned requirements of a particular release. The demand list target date may represent the date on which the list of functional and non-functional requirements listed in the product demand list must be completed.

The speed predictor 132 may implement supervised machine learning, including a seasonal trend decomposition (STL) model, which may represent a time series model. With respect to the selection of seasonal trend decomposition models, because correlations between influencing variables and target variables may not be established, a time series model may be used with the speed predictor 132. Further, because the variables may include enough data points with seasonality and trends, a seasonal trend decomposition model may be used for the speed predictor 132. Seasonal trend decomposition models may use historical data to provide modeling of seasonal and trend for future predictions.

According to an example, the first correct story predictor 136 may be executed by at least one hardware processor to determine a first correct story value for future releases and sprites. The first correct story may be described as: stories that can be completed and deployed into production without a single defect being recorded for them. More first correct stories may indicate higher product quality. Future releases may be described as: there is a scope to be completed, a release to be started on a future date. Future sprint (future iterations) may be described as: there is a range of iterations that the plan is to complete, starting at a future date. In this example, the first correct story predictor 136 may be executed by at least one hardware processor to determine a first correct story value based on a total number of user stories executed without a flaw divided by a total number of user stories executed. The user stories performed may be described as the number of user stories completed by a team.

The first time correct story predictor 136 may implement supervised machine learning, including a single exponential smoothing model that may represent a time series model. With respect to the selection of a single exponential smoothing model, a time series model may be used with the first correct story predictor 136 because correlations between influencing variables and target variables may not be established. Further, since the variables may not include enough data points, a single exponential smoothing model may be used for the first correct story predictor 136. A single exponential smoothing model may provide future expected values that assign more weight to the nearest value.

According to an example, story quality predictor 138 may be executed by at least one hardware processor to determine a number of defects per story for future releases and sprites. The defect of each story can be described as: for the approximate number of defects that the story was posed. In this example, the story quality predictor 138 may be executed by at least one hardware processor to determine the number of defects per story based on a total number of defects associated with a story executed for at least one of a particular sprint or post divided by a total number of stories executed for the at least one of a particular sprint or post.

Story quality predictor 138 may implement supervised machine learning, including a single exponential smoothing model that may represent a time series model. With respect to the selection of a single exponential smoothing model, a time series model may be used with story quality predictor 138 because correlations between influencing variables and target variables may not be established. Further, a single exponential smoothing model may be used for story quality predictor 138, as the variables may not include enough data points. A single exponential smoothing model may provide future expected values that assign more weight to the nearest value.

According to an example, the commitment accuracy predictor 142 may be executed by at least one hardware processor to determine a commitment accuracy value for future releases and sprints. The commitment accuracy value may be described as a value indicating the accuracy of the commitment of the iteration (e.g., (total story point completed/total story point committed) ×100). In this example, commitment accuracy predictor 142 may be executed by at least one hardware processor to determine a commitment accuracy value from a speed estimation accuracy value determined from a completed total story point divided by a committed total story point and a workload estimation accuracy value determined from a planned total workload divided by an actual total workload. The total story point completed may be described as: sum of story points of stories the team has completed so far.
